summary: Lists the parameters used by ASAP and ENRP, the protocols in the Reliable Server Pooling architecture. It collects the values and registrations those protocols need, so they can be implemented consistently. It is published as an experimental document.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a reference sheet listing the codes and settings that two related protocols agree to use, so different programs can talk to each other.

subtitle: Reference parameters for ASAP and ENRP protocols.

tldr.problem: ASAP and ENRP protocols need to communicate consistently across different implementations. They require a shared set of parameter types, transport protocols, and error codes.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines and registers all the Type-Length-Value parameters and error causes used by ASAP and ENRP. It collects 16 parameter types covering addresses, transports, and policies, plus 11 error codes.
tldr.outcome: Implementations can follow this registry to ensure compatible message exchange. This is part of the Reliable Server Pooling architecture for high-availability services.

today: RFC 5354 is an Experimental protocol. It specifies the parameter registry for ASAP and ENRP, which themselves remain experimental. These protocols are part of the Reliable Server Pooling (RSerPool) architecture for high-availability applications.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
ASAP (Aggregate Server Access Protocol) and ENRP (Endpoint Handlespace Redundancy Protocol) are two companion protocols that work together to provide a high-availability, data-transfer mechanism over IP networks. They share many common parameters in their message formats.

This RFC is a reference document that details all the common message parameters shared between the two protocols. It provides parameter formats only; for how to use them, refer to RFC 5352 (ASAP) and RFC 5353 (ENRP). All parameters are transmitted in network byte order (big-endian).
sections.plainLanguage: Two protocols need to talk to each other using agreed-upon codes and message layouts. This document lists all those codes and layouts so they can communicate correctly.

sections.title: Parameter and Message Structure
sections.content:
All parameters use a Type-Length-Value (TLV) format. Each parameter starts with a 16-bit type field (identifying what kind of data it is), followed by a 16-bit length field (how many bytes it contains), then the actual data, padded to align on 4-byte boundaries.

The parameter type field uses its two highest bits to specify how to handle unrecognized parameters: stop and discard, stop and report an error, skip and continue, or skip and report an error. This allows future extensions without breaking old implementations.

Messages themselves follow a similar structure: an 8-bit message type, 8-bit flags, 16-bit length, and a variable-length message value. Messages are also padded to 4-byte alignment.
sections.plainLanguage: Data is packaged like a labeled box: the label says what's inside, a number says how big it is, and then comes the data. Extra space is padded so everything lines up neatly.

sections.title: Address and Transport Parameters
sections.content:
The RFC defines six transport protocol parameters: DCCP, SCTP, TCP, UDP, and UDP-Lite. Each carries a port number and one or more IP addresses. SCTP is special because it can list multiple addresses; the others support one IP address each.

Additionally, IPv4 and IPv6 Address parameters carry individual network addresses in binary form. IPv4 addresses are 32 bits; IPv6 addresses are 128 bits.

SCTP and ASAP transport parameters include a Transport Use field indicating whether the transport is for data only or for both data and control messages. Other transports are always data-only.
sections.plainLanguage: To send data to another computer, you need to know where it is (its address) and which door to knock on (its port). These parameters describe addresses and ports for different types of network pipes.

sections.title: Pool Policies and Server Information
sections.content:
The RFC defines a Pool Member Selection Policy parameter that specifies which server in a pool should be chosen when a client asks for service. The actual policy types are defined in RFC 5356 and include round-robin, weighted round-robin, random, priority-based, and load-based policies.

A Pool Handle parameter names a pool (a group of servers), and a Pool Element parameter describes one server, including its ID, registration lifetime, user transport, selection policy, and ASAP control transport. The Server Information parameter describes an ENRP server itself, holding its ID and transport address.
sections.plainLanguage: When you need a cashier, the store has rules for which cashier serves you: maybe they take turns (round-robin) or you pick randomly. Pool parameters describe these rules and which servers belong to which group.

sections.title: Error Reporting
sections.content:
The RFC defines an Operation Error parameter for reporting problems. It carries one or more error causes, each with a 16-bit cause code and detailed information. Eleven error causes are registered: unspecified error, unrecognized parameter, unrecognized message, invalid values, non-unique pool element identifier, inconsistent pool policy, lack of resources, inconsistent transport type, inconsistent data/control configuration, rejection due to security, and unknown pool handle.

Additional support parameters include a Cookie parameter (opaque state), a PE Identifier parameter (unique server ID), a PE Checksum parameter (integrity check over pool elements), and an Opaque Transport parameter (application-specific data).
sections.plainLanguage: When something goes wrong, the protocol sends an error message saying what happened. These are the standard error messages both protocols understand.

fields.name: Parameter Type
fields.desc: Identifies the parameter type; the two highest bits control unrecognized handling.

fields.name: Parameter Length
fields.desc: Total length including Type, Length, Value and padding.

items.label: Stop, discard
items.desc: Stop processing and discard the message.

items.label: Stop and report
items.desc: Stop and send an error about the unrecognized parameter.

items.label: Skip
items.desc: Skip this parameter and continue processing.

items.label: Skip and report
items.desc: Skip and report an error about the unrecognized parameter.
